of the term forecasting system. We present a novel hybrid approach that integrates 
Bayesian and latent modeling to enhance term forecasting accuracy within 
the Iranian Persian language. The proposed model leverages latent semantic data 
and term co-occurrence patterns to determine an optimal term distribution. 
Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this model, as confirmed 
by comparative analysis of the F-score metric. Additionally, we investigate 
the impact of varying parameter values on the proposed model's performance.

Recent advancements in sessions have shown that sequence of user interactions can be forecasted using sequential suggestion techniques. These approaches are particularly effective in environments where numerous items are involved and prior history is taken into consideration. To tackle these challenges, a new framework, called TwoPhase Sessions, has been developed to address the complexity of offering recommendations to users one item at a time. This framework builds upon RankNet, a learning to rank model, by incorporating two-phase training, utilizing both paired and unaligned data in a collaborative filtering manner. As a result, TwoPhase Sessions outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, demonstrating substantial improvements of up to 260% when tested on two diverse datasets. Furthermore, by integrating this framework into a real-world e-commerce system, it was discovered that TwoPhase Sessions increased sales by applying the suggested items to user sessions, demonstrating significant practical value in the industry.

Recent research on active matter, representing drive mechanisms through activity coefficients, not thermal energy, has yielded substantial knowledge on active particles, often overlooked in traditional thermodynamic models. In this work, a non-Newtonian fluid with activity fluctuating in space acts as the substrate for a collective of actively deformed colloidal discs, observed employing active particle simulation, expanding the scope of existing models. By mapping the flow to an effective Newtonian fluid model, considering activity fluctuations, we have determined, through theoretical and numerical methods, the critical force at which the active particles undergo a sudden shape change, transforming into a complete circle. Additionally, we have investigated the impact of varying activity levels on these active particles, observed altering their behavior in response to changing activity coefficients. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that, in the absence of activity, our results seamlessly reconcile the observed behavior with existing simulations, utilizing thermal energy as the driving mechanism.

A novel multi-dimensional network fracture model is presented, in which fractures are represented by nodes and edges of a graph. We demonstrate the efficacy of a versatile modeling approach, employing the mimetic finite variation method within a conforming network fracture model. This involves mapping conservative variables to fracture edges via conformal projections. We explore the transition of flow from one fracture to another and calculate the flow rate as fractures intersect. Diverse test cases are used to validate our approach, including single fracturing domains and multiple fracturing domains separated by large distances, which require the resolution of relative pressures and potential differences. These scenarios involve either duality or multi-dimensional network fractures, which may be parallel or perpendicular to each other. We examine the models' performance with three sets of synthetic fractures: (1) arbitrarily oriented and spaced fractures, (2) simultaneously created horizontal and vertically oriented fractures, and (3) a group of horizontally spaced fractures. In each case, our models accurately replicate the behavior of three-dimensional discrete fracture tensor block models, matching the flow rates and converging to the same results. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability of our models to solve single fracturing domain problems to the same level of accuracy as other methods, using much fewer grid elements. This saves processing time, as shown by computational examples.

This study introduces an innovative approach for aligning a swarm of autonomous drones with a dynamic human crowd while maintaining its distinctive organizational structure. Our proposed algorithm proactively avoids collisions with crowd members by seamlessly shifting the swarm's trajectory to miss human obstacles. Both the swarm of drones and the crowd are represented by sets of points in three-dimensional space, and the alignment process minimizes the similarity between their respective geometric features. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of our method in preserving the swarm's original pattern, preventing collisions, and reducing alignment time, especially when dealing with complex and dynamic environments.

A matrix sequence, also known as a matrix sequence of connections, is constructed from a graph's Seidel energy by applying the Fibonacci sequence in a recursive manner.  We have determined both the range of Seidel energy and asymptotic numerical values for the Fibonacci polynomial coefficients in a recent study.  We have further found that certain matrix sequences of connection types are equivalent to well-known special types of matrices.  Specifically, we have found three distinct cases where the matrix sequence of connection types is equivalent to the Chebyshev polynomials, the ultraspherical polynomials, and the Gegenbauer polynomials, respectively.  We have also shown that a particular type of graph, sequence graphs, is associated with a stable range of Seidel energy.  We have further proven an asymptotic expression for the Fibonacci polynomial coefficients in the form of n-1, as n approaches infinity.  This is in addition to a particular case of the Fibonacci polynomial coefficients in the form of (n-1)^k, as k approaches infinity.

The paper addresses a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations with delays (SDDEs) driven by a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter greater than 0.5, under assumptions ensuring the existence and smoothness of solutions to both the state and control equations. We establish a key result showing that for a broad class of costs, the optimal solution can be represented as the solution to a finite-dimensional optimization problem, and this result is further validated for two specific examples, one stemming from a telegraph process, and the other related to a multi-agent system of delayed interacting particles.

We examine a one-dimensional Dirac operator with a non-self-adjoint nature and a potential that contains a coercive component, which forms part of a larger model studied in population dynamics. A potential V represents the effects of population growth and interaction. The article delves into the existence and structure of the finite-band Hilbert space H γ, the completion of C 0,1 functions, where the operator's spectrum is contained within a bounded interval. We prove that H γ supports an orthonormal basis consisting of real, positive functions, which forms the basis of a simple, non-self-adjoint graph theory applicable to the operator's compact perturbations.

The development of vehicular networks is a vital aspect of the Internet of Things, with researchers exerting significant effort to enhance vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communications. To address the limitations of vehicle reliability and coverage, this work investigates the potential of utilizing road-side units (RSUs) and vehicle relays (VRs) with the ability to surpass vehicle speed. A proposed framework models a tiered vehicular network as a hierarchical geographically distributed system, with RSUs and VRs acting as local mini-hubs. By analyzing the effects of vehicle density, speed, and flow on network performance, simulations demonstrate that VRs significantly improve network reliability and reduce the impact of vehicle flow.

Wikipedia's vast knowledge base relies heavily on community contributions, with articles undergoing constant improvement. Our research focuses on identifying and categorizing Wikipedia articles that require revision using patterns in editing behavior, rather than relying on the content itself. By analyzing metadata, we're able to pinpoint articles with low quality issues accurately, and our proposed method demonstrates significant improvement over existing approaches in accurately classifying articles with problems, a task that proves to be a difficult machine learning problem. Our findings reveal that editors actively maintain articles with low quality issues, and that previous research has overlooked the vital role these individuals play in order to develop effective strategies for enhancing article quality. Our research also yields a useful tool for automatically labeling low quality Wikipedia articles, and our results demonstrate that incorporating data from Wikipedia's Polish edition, which has a higher percentage of articles with problems, enhances the performance of our system.

Recent studies have discovered that deep neural networks (DNNs) can incorporate inner-workings like reasoning rules, making them suitable for tasks such as knowledge graph link prediction. Nonetheless, there's limited research exploring the incorporation of decision-based reasoning rules in DNNs. We've found that training DNNs with a small subset of true decisions and fake ones (from a diversified set) enhances their ability to learn these decisions. Furthermore, the utilization of dropout during training increases the diversity of learned decisions, leading to better generalization. We've applied this approach successfully to link prediction in knowledge graphs and semi-supervised sentiment analysis.

The process of undocked $B^0_s$ mesons decaying into $\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ or $\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ combinations has been investigated using data collected by the LHCb experiment, equivalent to 1.6 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity, taken at proton-proton collisions with centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV. A significant decay ratio indicating the presence of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ transitions over $\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ transitions is reported for the first time, with a measured ratio equivalent to $0.206 \pm 0.017 \pm 0.013 \pm 0.003$. Furthermore, a preference for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ over $\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ transitions is observed with a measured relative ratio of $0.061 \pm 0\,026 \pm 0.011$.

We've extended traditional T-duality from compact Lie group symmetries to more complex geometric settings, applying it to twisted torus configurations. Our method leverages a novel representation of the Lie algebra, one that incorporates the twisted flux form as a basic element, thereby generating the full Lie algebra through its Lie bracket operation. This approach allows us to clearly define geometric T-duality in various forms, including the full differential form formulation. As an example, we've applied our method to a situation involving a five-dimensional anti-de Sitter bulk space, where we demonstrated the existence of a dual dual metric. Additionally, we've established that geometric T-duality preserves certain characteristics of supersymmetric solutions, thereby defining a new subset of such solutions within the general supergravity framework.

Recent advances in collaborative learning through observation have shown promising results, with the majority of research focusing on pre-trained models and relying on extensive expert demonstrations in the target domain. In this study, we address two key limitations of existing work: (a) the reliance on extensive expert input and (b) the necessity of pre-trained models. Our proposed approach, COPL, utilizes only unlabelled data from multiple sources and develops observational knowledge without relying on expert examples. Furthermore, COPL is model-agnostic, with the ability to adapt from any starting point, whether untrained or previously trained in a separate process. Our experiments across three domains of real-world interest demonstrate that COPL is able to form useful observational knowledge and can operate without expert input, with performance comparable to that achieved through pre-trained models.

PAC codes are designed to correct a predetermined number of parallel channel errors, with each channel having its unique error pattern. Unlike conventional codes, which often assume independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) channel errors, PAC codes can handle distinct error types in parallel channels. We explore the evaluation of PAC code performance using error metrics such as the Hammer price function, and find that certain codes exhibit optimal performance in specific scenarios. Additionally, our study delves into the computational challenges of decoding PAC codes and outlines a potential complexity-benefit analysis to guide future research and development.

We tackle the complex task of simultaneously tracking multiple hand poses and
object positions in a cloud of point data, all while the hands are in grasp postures.
To accomplish this, we employ a hand modeling approach that includes rigid hand meshes and
predicts hand segmentations, as well as an object detection and reconstruction system.
Our proposed method streamlines the solution by leveraging the inherent hand stability
when hands wrap around objects, allowing us to optimize hand pose and object pose jointly.
Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate our method surpasses state-of-the-art
approaches and even matches or surpasses human performance in many cases. Moreover, our
method's efficiency enables real-time processing of dataset data, making it suitable for
real-world and household PC environments. To facilitate reproducibility, our source code,
3D models, and pre-trained models are all available for download at the specified links.

A type of geometric figure known as a rank 4 C-configuration with a 120-degree angle and a symmetry order of 5 can be used to create certain patterns of triangles called rank 4 C-collections with a 120-degree angle and a symmetry order of 5, when replicated in a plane divided into 20 identical sections, resulting in a pattern that shows a link between these rank 4 C-collections and the Coxeter groups of types A4, D4, and G2. By duplicating this in a plane divided into different numbers of sections, we can study the properties of the associated permutation groups, which have a rank 4 C-configuration as their fundamental source, meaning they are based on this basic shape. We find that our rank 4 C-collections with a 120-degree angle and a symmetry order of 5, when replicated in a plane divided into 22 sections, are actually reflectums of a special type of triangle called a rank 4 A-configuration with a 120-degree angle, which has a symmetry order of 10. This means that our rank 4 C-collections with a 120-degree angle and a symmetry order of 5, when replicated in a plane divided into 22 sections, are not unique and have a connection to the Coxeter groups of types A4, D4, and G2. Furthermore, we study the properties of the associated permutation groups, which have a rank 4 C-configuration as

A robot can be quickly set up in a room by using a depth camera without the need for a marker, by developing a novel algorithm that determines the correct position of the depth camera and the location of the end-effector. This algorithm works in real-time, with data from the depth camera being processed to create a 3D map of the environment and the position of the robot being calculated using an advanced algorithm, with the results showing a high level of accuracy. The time taken for the setup process was significantly cut down, with an accuracy rate of 0.02 degrees and 0.02 meters in a complex, real-world test setup.

A novel framework has been developed to analyze the causal effects of treatment in the presence of interference, where the response is a multivariate outcome. The concept of treatment disruption is also explored within this framework by establishing conditions for its identification. Under the assumed interdependence structure, wherein adjacent units receive the same treatment, a novel consistent estimator has been proposed for the interference parameter. The theoretical justification for our approach involves proving the asymptotic accuracy of the estimator. The utility of our method has been demonstrated through applications in multivariate linear models and simulated data sets. Additionally, the proposed method has been applied to analyze treatment disruption in social networks.

The primary neutrino emissions from dark matter encounters with nuclei may hold considerable value in understanding both dark matter and stellar phenomena. In this research, the neutrino production mechanisms within neutron stars are investigated, focusing on collisions involving a scalar field responsible for conjugate symmetry breaking. The study takes into account the actual spectrum of this scalar field as it pertains to the symmetry breaking process. The calculation of neutrino emissions induced by this field is carried out utilizing both relativistic and non-relativistic nucleons. The results indicate that in certain mass ranges, the neutrino production can be substantially higher than previously estimated. The prediction of accelerated cooling rates in neutron stars could provide a basis for validating or refuting the hypothesis of dark matter encounters through neutrino observations.

The ongoing UNIONS/CFIS survey is conducting the most comprehensive morphological cataloging effort to date at $20r$ magnitude in the Northern Galactic Plane with accurate measurements of elliptical shapes. To process the large dataset, an automated pipeline, ShapePipe, utilizes multiple techniques to optimize shape detection and analysis. The pipeline's final catalog demonstrates exceptional performance with high accuracy and robust results across various magnitude ranges. By employing ShapePipe, we generated a CFIS shape catalog that spans from $20r$ to $23r$ magnitude, achieving a 0.04 percent error in elliptical shape measurements. Applying this catalog to weak-lensing analysis of the galaxy cluster, MC2J133124.6+295044, yields a signal-to-noise ratio of $40.1$ for the mass reconstruction, consistent with X-ray data. Furthermore, ShapePipe successfully detected the systematics associated with galaxy morphology in the CFIS data. With its versatile design and multiple configuration options, ShapePipe is adept at handling distinct data sets.

We offer an innovative proof of Weyl's original hypothesis for nonrectangular Kronecker-Weyl systems with a specific property, in addition to extending a current result by Merzel. A novel estimate is also presented that answers a question posed by Yucel Yilmaz.

We demonstrate that for k-rational local complete intersections, k-Du Bois, k-rational, and k-Du Bois local complete unions are interchangeable terms. Moreover, in conjunction with Cluckers' and Loeser's findings, this implies k-rational local complete unions have an exponential integral in the sense of Beckmann, and thus, are also k-Du Bois and k-rational.

Our investigation focuses on the analysis of magnetic properties of a specifically designed chain of spin-1/2 ions, where Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless phase behavior is adjustable by an applied magnetic field. This property allows the number of low-lying spin excitations to vary in response to the field, thereby affecting the temperature range in which the ordered state transitions into a disordered phase. This goal-driven approach is exemplified in a study of the compound [Cu(NCMe)4]BF4, which exhibits BKT phase behavior as a function of both temperature and magnetic field intensity.

Recent findings from the DES luminosity survey and other sources suggest that dark matter may have lower density in the vicinity of galaxies. We hypothesize that this phenomenon can be attributed to 1) the accumulation of massive stars' remnant cores, 2) neutrinos, and 3) ultralight bosons, including axions, within the galaxies' gravitational influence. Focusing on the axion option, we explore a scenario in which a large number of axions form a coherent wave, known as an "oscillon", within galaxies' potential wells. This condition is feasible if primordial oscillions were created soon after the universe's birth and weigh as much as stars. We have developed a numerical approach to simulate oscillon formation for diverse wave types and have determined that a coherent wave with a 1 solar mass radius and a 10^-6 M_s^2 mass scales' amplitude can stabilize within the galaxy's boundary. We derive mathematical equations for the stability of oscillons in steady-state conditions and analyze their behavior over time. Notably, we find that oscillons with larger scales tend to remain stable for extended periods, which could lead to a scenario in which the universe's matter distribution appears lower at smaller (galaxy-scale) and higher (large-scale) areas, if the scales of oscillon stability align with these two regimes.

Quantum computing advocates for utilizing exotic quantum states like the Gaudin states, which exhibit exceptional properties. Specifically, the Gaudin states, formed by two spin-1/2 particles, are known to have an upper limit on the rank of their stabilizer space that grows quadratically with the number of particles. Research aimed to quantify this rank's upper limit led to the introduction of the \textit{stabilizer rank} in the study of quantum information. This paper delves into the computational complexity of determining the stabilizer rank of a general quantum state. Notably, the problem is shown to be NP-hard, even when restricted to specific, classical-quantum forms. Building upon this finding, we develop two new protocol-specific constraints that can facilitate faster resolution of the stabilizer rank in certain scenarios. Specifically, we introduce enhanced upper limits (EULs) for the stabilizer rank of magic states, which significantly surpass prior estimates. These EULs are derived through a deeper understanding of the structure of these states within the Gaudin matrix, along with the creation and anti_creation matrices.

This study utilizes the Tsallis holographic dark energy model to derive an expression for thermal radiation entropy in the complex quintessence framework. Building upon Tsallis' previous work, the model leads to a generalised entropy concept, adhering to the classical idea at the point of p = 1. The model's analysis involves calculating the harmonic density functions, Adjoint representation, and radial distribution functions in accordance with quantum statistics. Notably, we demonstrate that our calculations yield consistent results whether approached from a microcanonical, canonical, or grand canonical framework. Furthermore, we illustrate the effects of variation in parameters on thermal radiation entropy using graphical representations. In addition, we examine the relationship between entropy and temperature in the complex quintessence framework.

The Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Telescope (LAMOST) employed the Variable Star Observatory to track asterosecular variations in several regions, specifically in the fields LAMOST Object 668451-674515 and GD 1976, which exhibit non-adiabatic variability in the field LAMOST Object 673116-680135, and in the field LAMOST Object 685226-690225, which shows both official designation variability and amateur observations. These studies utilized four $K$2 plates from LAMOST's fifth observing run to identify 1573 stars, which were then analyzed using the AMOEBA algorithm to obtain initial results, including their light curves and characteristics.

A novel technique called TuRaN involves generating truly random binary sequences by intentionally reducing the voltage to a dynamically randomized SRAM array while it's being written. To stabilize the SRAM's state during this process, the rising edge of the next clock cycle is captured and formatted into a random binary sequence. Unlike traditional TRNGs, which rely on electronic randomness sources, TuRaN leverages physical randomness caused by process variations and voltage scaling to generate its random digits. Additionally, TuRAN incurs minimal overhead as it utilizes existing circuit components and doesn't necessitate any additional hardware. Our experiments, carried out on 28nm technology nodes, demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in producing high-entropy binary sequences. Furthermore, TuRAN has been successfully implemented in several systems, including FPGA and SoC devices.

A reliable system for controlling the electronic communications between components at the molecular level is crucial for the development of ultra-dense, high-performance electronic systems. We have designed and simulated a single-electron relay molecule that serves this purpose. This molecule features a compact structure with a large electronic barrier between two parts. It's possible for the barrier height to adjust based on the position of a central anchor group, allowing for a transition between two stable states when a small electric charge is added. Our study demonstrates that this molecule operates as an effective switch in a circuit when connected to a set of quantum dots and shows stable behavior over a wide range of conditions. Additionally, we've found that this molecule is resistant to the effects of environmental fluctuations and can be used as part of a larger system for managing data transmission at the molecular level.

We develop a novel representation of multi-loop scattering amplitudes in a form that conforms to Einstein's causality, where all particles' imaginary parts are positive. Our framework is grounded in the principles of loop-level unitarity and features a series of integrals with scalar denominators that progressively simplify with increasing loop order. Building upon a recent formula involving discrete causal integration, we derive a comprehensive expression for correlators of four scalar fields around a flat spacetime, marking the highest multi-loop achievement to date in this domain. Our calculations are executed using a computer algebra system and are validated through multiple analyses, including a direct comparison with a publicly accessible causal integral library. This work has implications in both particle physics and AdS/CFT correspondence, where a causal amplitude may be linked to a conformal correlation function.

We've developed an expression to extend one-dimensional two-state quantum stride eigenfunctions to cover all spatial values. This formulation applies to any given energy level 'E', where 'k' is a wave number, 't' is time, and 'γ(t)' is a time-dependent coupling parameter based on the sum of exponentials with varying frequencies and phases. The derived eigenfunction expression can be applied to both positive and negative 'k' ranges, where we have specifically analyzed the behavior of eigenfunctions for 'k = 0' and shown that certain conditions lead to non-exponential decay or growth patterns in this context.

In a theoretical framework, nuclear and quark matter phases are modeled using different density functions to describe their behavior. This research investigates the composition and structure of celestial bodies consisting of two distinct matter phases, where one phase is a nuclear matter and the other is a quark matter, and their interfaces are analyzed. The study focuses on hybrid celestial bodies, which are stable only when their gravitational force balances their internal pressure. Theoretical models, such as the sigma-omega-rho paradigm combined with the MIT and NJL models, are employed to examine the globular ultraslowly rotating neutron stars.

This study explores optomechanical interactions within a $q$-deformed system, comprising of two deformed cavities that interact with a single mechanical mirror and external driving fields. We examine the optomechanical coupling under both conservative and dissipative conditions, focusing on how optomechanical coupling and driving field affect light transmittance, amplification, speed, and optimization within the system. Our results indicate that the $q$-deformation has a significant impact on optomechanical interactions, where $q$-nonlinearity enables the transmission and amplification of light even beyond the $q=1$ scenario, and that by properly selecting optomechanical coupling and driving power, enhanced transmission and amplification can be achieved for both fast and slowly moving light.

Researchers have found that the Double-Rotors Model, which incorporates R-parity into a model of two rotating objects with different colors, can be linked to the Adverse R-parity Scissors Mode phenomenon. Specifically, as the R-parity breaks, the system's density distributes unevenly across the two objects, resulting in the development of spatial deformations and angular momenta differences between them. In the Double-Rotors Model, this Adverse R-parity Scissors Mode phenomenon is characterized by an irregular change in the system's density, mirrored by separate R-colored components, which becomes more pronounced as the break in R-parity accelerates. In the region of large R-parity breakages, the Double-Rotors Model exhibits behavior similar to the Central Cracked Coulomb Gain phenomenon, whereas in regions of slow R-parity breakages, the model exhibits the traditional R-parity Scissors Mode phenomenon, characterized by the system's angular momentum exceeding its parent's by one.

Thin layers of metal oxides exhibit unique properties originating from complex charge fluctuations across ultra-thin boundaries, which can manifest as varying spin states. Research has been conducted using spectroscopic analysis to examine the spin and orbital fluctuations in ultra-thin layers of iron oxide, specifically in the low-pressure range. Results demonstrate a gradual increase in spin fluctuations as the thickness of the iron oxide layers decreases. Furthermore, a notable peak associated with spin fluctuations is observed to shift towards a higher binding energy as the thickness diminishes. Orbital fluctuations, characterized by a specific energy level, also exhibit a thickness-dependent trend within the iron oxide layers. In addition, a significant increase in intensity associated with orbital fluctuations is identified within the same pressure range. These findings are substantiated by theoretical computations, which confirm the existence of spin and orbital fluctuations across ultra-thin iron oxide layers.

The behavior of particles under dissipative optical lattices is of great interest. A general model has been developed to study this phenomenon, which, for specific conditions, mirrors the results obtained from the Hartree-Bose-Hubbard model. A case study of atoms cooled by a laser reveals that, when trapped, their number distribution often follows a non-Gaussian pattern. The exceptions to this rule are found in two scenarios, such as, dense regimes or intense laser conditions. The resulting distributions are either symmetric or negatively skewed. The origin of these anomalies is understood by analyzing the particles' cooling process and their resulting spatial patterns. The theoretical findings are corroborated by numerical simulations of the cold-atom experiment.

Cryptocurrencies have proliferated as a alternative to traditional financial systems, with their trading networks characterised by dynamic interplay between numerous cryptocurrencies. By constructing a multi-layer network based on trading pair creation times, researchers uncovered various trading strategies, underlying trends, and market segments. Analyzing time-evolving network properties allowed for the identification of significant periods in cryptocurrency trading and diversification in investment strategies. Furthermore, the diverse trends in different layers of the network pointed to the presence of multiple regimes in cryptocurrency investment. A cross-validation test was used to evaluate the reliability of their findings and guide future research.

The formation of small sulfuric acid clusters plays a significant role in atmospheric chemistry. The presence of abundant water in the atmosphere could facilitate the coalescence of sulfuric acid molecules into larger particles able to support condensational growth, thus affecting cloud formation and precipitation. Utilizing simulations with quantum mechanical movements to account for temperature fluctuations, the study examines the structure, energy, and dipole moment of sulfuric acid and water clusters ranging from 3 to 15 molecules. At room temperature, stable dimer and larger sulfuric acid clusters are typically separated, with the acid molecules oriented in a row (providing a mechanism for growth), whereas monomers and small clusters have significant dipole moments. When accounting for temperature fluctuations, the typical separation distance in dimer clusters increases, although they remain relatively close. The presence of water molecules disrupts this structure, creating larger clusters, and reduces the dipole moment. These findings demonstrate the significance of utilizing zero-point energy in simulating tiny sulfuric acid and water clusters, and suggest that stable dimer structures with separated acid molecules could serve as building blocks for the coalescence of sulfuric acid molecules into larger particles, with water molecules facilitating this process by disrupting acid clusters and reducing their dipole moments.

We establish the exact definition of a compactification of pairs of categories, which consists of the union of isomorphism classes of functors from these pairs of categories to the category of finite sets, and the corresponding topological properties. It is proven that this compactification can be embedded into the space of matrices representing maps from one pair of categories to another, equipped with the topology of convergence of finite values, which in turn forms a countable Polshkov space, and thus a metrizable, compact space. Building on this result, we find the compactification of the space of operators on a finite set, and those on a finite set, symmetric matrices. Additionally, we determine the compactification of the space of operators on a finite set that are invariant under a specific group, and find its topology, and finally, we find the compactification of the space of operators on a finite set that are invariant under a specific group, and describe its geometry.

Holographic thermal Hall effect experiments demonstrate that the thermal Hall conductive rate can exceed the charge conductive rate, contradicting Einstein's predictions. We've discovered that this anomaly is primarily caused by the inaccuracy of Newton's gravitational analogues at the boundary of the black hole for models where the boundary components have non-zero curvature. For situations with vanishing curvature, the thermal Hall conductive rate is found to be lower than the charge conductive rate, and it's proportional to the charge conductive rate. We've also found that the heat conductive rate can exceed the charge conductive rate in systems without curvature, and we've developed a general formula for the ratio of the thermal Hall conductive rate to the charge conductive rate in these cases.

In various machine learning tasks, overparameterized neural networks consistently achieve straightforward solutions with minimal training data. Our work explores how network architecture and data dimensionality interact to produce these simple solutions, and we identify multiple factors that contribute to their success. These factors include the complexity of network weights, grouping properties, and the geometric structure of data, which are all influenced by the network architecture. With a greater number of parameters, the tendency to encounter simple solutions increases, as the interactions between these factors produce diverse and complex representations, facilitating generalization. Notably, different network architectures can produce identical geometric structures in the data, and we demonstrate that the quasicrystalline structure, in particular, leads to successful generalization. Our findings are supported by experiments in both training neural networks and the solution of differential equations.

We have established a novel strategy to determine the Wilson coefficients of semileptonic $B$-meson decays that suffer from uncertainness stemming from missing theoretical predictions of related hadronic interactions. Our proposed method employs the exclusive $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decay as a reference point to make use of the well-defined branching ratio and its distribution over several kinematic parameters. As new data from $B$-factories and LHCb continue to flow in, we show how this information can be used to extract Wilson coefficients with high precision, using a likelihood fit that takes into account all available Wilson coefficients simultaneously. Our results indicate that a single-month's worth of Wilson coefficient data from $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ can rival the current Wilson coefficient information derived from $B\to \bar B\gamma\gamma$ decays, providing significant benefits for the New Physics searches in semileptonic $B$-meson decays.

Recent breakthroughs in transformer-based models have led to superior music generation results, but they struggle with evaluating composed music. To address this, we utilize transformer architectures for both boosting input data quality and constructing a comprehensive music representation, which ultimately facilitates reliable evaluation of composed music. Moreover, our approach is characterized by its minimal additions to the basic transformer model, making it a practical solution for using existing pre-trained music models. Experimental findings confirm that our strategy significantly improves the performance of music composition evaluation models.

The use of copula models has become increasingly common due to their flexibility in expressing joint probability distributions through marginal probability distributions and dependence information. This note provides a summary of recent developments in copula models, focusing on models that analyze only marginal dependencies, which are naturally represented by copulas. It also discusses the challenges of estimating dependence parameters within these models and explores the role of optimal transport methods in this process.

A prospective distribution theory is developed to study mobility between economic states in a multi-agent, multi-state environment. The theory is based on an assumption of preference for higher intergenerational income equality. To achieve this, a parent's or ancestor's economic status is valued at some level of persistence, averaging the states of their ancestors or descendants over a finite period. The minimum amount of inheritance needed for a certain level of economic stability in the future is calculated, and it is found that the Gini index is affected by state-transmission probabilities and the memory length in the network. A general method is also provided to calculate the expected values of all possible paths in a multi-agent, multi-state network.

The link between spin and statistics is traditionally grounded in the application of the commutator algebra as outlined in the Pauli principle. This relationship will be reestablished, yet alternatively, by utilizing the parity operator and a non-relativistic framework. The key assumption in this revelatory approach is the derivation of the total wave function from charge and current densities, where the latter is expressed in terms of a relativistic P-odd vector. From this foundation, the constraints on spin and statistics will be deduced, where the spin quantum number is determined by the parity of the angular momentum, and the statistics quantum number is derived from the commutator of these operators, which generates both positive and negative integers, corresponding to bosons and fermions, respectively.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in the Delegated RingCT protocol. The Delegated RingCT protocol is adaptable to various dPoS-based cryptocurrencies. Our work focuses on improving the financial privacy of these cryptocurrencies by mitigating address visible transactions. To this end, we describe an efficient Delegated RingCT implementation in two commonly used programming languages and then evaluate its performance on test networks. Our tests using the Rust-based Substrate framework reveal that Delegated RingCT transactions significantly outperform traditional ring signatures transactions by at least 10 times, while also being more versatile. Additionally, our work outlines a potential framework for integrating Delegated RingCT into existing dPoS blockchain implementations.

A significant issue in numerous scientific applications, such as computer tomography and radio astronomy, is reducing large datasets from multiple sources into a single image, a process that involves solving an underdetermined linear equation. Characterizing the solvability of such equations, particularly in an geometric framework, is essential. We investigated the theoretical foundations of solving these equations by analyzing the algebraic geometry of the system's zeros. Our study introduces concepts like 'tangency degree' and 'zero-clearing degree' and proves that the combinatorial complexity of solving these equations is tied to the embeddedness of the data's projection onto the torus. These findings lead to a theoretical assessment of the solvability of these equations, presenting both positive and negative results that illustrate the effect of the data's location in the torus on solvability. We validate our findings through various numerical experiments.

The first observation of three gauge bosons simultaneously produced and traveling in diverse directions was made using the LHCb detector, which operates at the LHC. This was done by collecting 9.4 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at a 13 TeV energy, yielding 3.5 standard deviations above background expectations. Multiple production mechanisms for the bosons are possible, including resonant production of heavy particles and non-resonant interactions resulting from the hard scattering of quarks and gluons.

In 2019, the Hebrew Universal Dependencies treebank was introduced, however it suffered from low quality annotations, primarily due to the lack of modern Hebrew text available online. This paper announces the updated UD Hebrew treebank with enhanced annotations, incorporating recent Hebrew text from various sources, such as news articles and social media platforms. The updated treebank now spans over 7,000 sentences, and a neural network parser trained on the new annotations demonstrates significant improvements in performance, achieving an F-score of 94% on the test set, compared to the previous parser's 52% F-score on the original annotation's training set.

We establish that for any $p$ in the interval $1\le p <\infty$, a linear map from $\ell_p$ to $\ell_q$ with $1<p,q<\infty$ and $\frac{1}{p}<\frac{1}{q}\le 1$ is $\varepsilon$-isometric onto an $n$-dimensional subspace if and only if a related $\varepsilon$-isometric map from $\ell_p$ to $\ell_q$ can be identified with a linear map from $\ell_p$ to $\ell_q$ whose image is a $n$-dimensional subspace of $\ell_q$. This equates the problem of determining the smallest dimension for $\varepsilon$-isometric maps from $\ell_p$ to $\ell_q$ with the problem of determining the smallest dimension for $\varepsilon$-isometric maps from $\ell_p$ to $\ell_q$ that have their images contained in a $n$-dimensional subspace of $\ell_q$. We supply an explicit upper bound for the dimension in the latter case, which improves a recent result from [Gogyan 2019].

Recent advancements in collaborative learning have shown great promise in achieving accurate region-of-interest segmentation on a larger scale. However, we have observed that current methods may not perform optimally due to: (a) an uneven distribution of samples among participants; (b) the loss of participant-specific information during aggregation; and (c) the limited training data for each participant. To address these challenges, we have developed an innovative approach for collaborative deep learning called the Collaborative data-informed modeling (CDIM) approach. This method involves: (a) a balanced participation mechanism to mitigate sample disparity; (b) a proprietary map technique to preserve participant uniqueness; and (c) the integration of external knowledge to inform segmentation. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our CDIM approach, we have conducted extensive experiments on two publicly available datasets, the Cervix region-of-interest segmentation task, and a hypothetical study on COVID-19 infection in lymphocytes. These experiments have shown that CDIM is capable of producing accurate infections ground truth, which cannot be achieved through traditional collaborative learning methods.

This research presents a novel method for designing efficient LDPC codes that can withstand harsh environments like the binary erasure channel. The proposed scheme creates LDPC codes with unique properties, such as degree-degree connections in the parity-check matrix, which significantly reduces the complexity of designing LDPC codes while ensuring exceptional error-prone data transmission performance. The method is versatile and can be applied to various coding schemes, including cyclic codes, and offers a practical approach to the complex problem of LDPC code design, including complex cyclic networks.

A crucial system-level component safety technique called Fault Tolerant Control aims to preserve system performance despite faulty actuators to ensure safe operation. The technique involves designing a control strategy that relies on an innovative approach to system operation, where the overall system remains stable despite individual actuator malfunctions. In this study, multiple FTBC designs are proposed for a pair of coupled electro-mechanical plants, which are commonly found in aircraft and are prone to actuator failure. The FTBC designs are developed using a recently introduced method of system-level synthesis and this work highlights the benefits of this approach for creating safe performance.

A critical component in the development of post-quantum cryptography is the decoy-state quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol. Recently, a novel approach incorporating phase randomization (PR) and measurement settings has been introduced to enhance the efficiency of distilling keys in long-distance QKD networks. Specifically, this improved protocol employs the phase of signal states to be varied, whereas all other states maintain a fixed phase, thereby reducing the number of necessary measurement settings needed to achieve a predetermined key distillation efficiency. However, our research reveals that this optimized protocol is susceptible to a sophisticated form of attack devised by our team, which involves manipulating only the interferometric visibility of signal states while retaining the phases of other states. This sophisticated attack can successfully evade detection even when the most advanced eavesdropping detection methods are employed, leading to a significant reduction in the number of necessary measurement settings required for a predetermined key distillation efficiency. Specifically, our team found that this optimized protocol is vulnerable to a significant reduction in the number of necessary measurement settings of up to 87.5% under certain conditions.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training datasets. Our investigation looks into the impact of utilizing datasets of different sizes (four sizes: small, medium, large, and extra-large) on the learning in-context process with a 1.3 billion parameter model. Interestingly, our research finds that an unusually large training dataset can actually hinder performance in some cases, highlighting the need for a baseline assessment of more training data. Additionally, our study reveals significant variations in the influence of dataset size based on the task type, and explores the relationship between form of training data influence and the internal model structure through the use of model weights and knowledge acquisition patterns. Furthermore, our research finds that a strategy of merging and refining fine-tuning data on the fly can mitigate some of the negative effects of an overwhelming training dataset load, and that a high degree of diversity within the training datasets is required to achieve this level of memory augmentation.

Galaxy clusters are thought to have formed through the same processes that created larger web-like structures, namely the aggregation of smaller galaxy groups, which in turn, are thought to have originated from smaller entities. To understand the details of this aggregation process, researchers have developed computational models to study it. These models often disregard certain processes, such as magnetic fields and thermal energy transfer, in favor of more simplistic simulations, but our work shows that including these processes is essential to understanding the aggregation process. Our models reveal that when magnetic fields strengthen and radiative cooling weathers the clouds, smaller galaxy groups are less likely to aggregate successfully. However, introducing thermal energy transfer helps to mitigate this effect, allowing successful aggregations to occur. Our results also highlight the importance of cloud fragmentation, which significantly affects the final structure of the aggregates. Ultimately, our study shows that computing models of galaxy cluster formation must take into account a variety of processes if they are to accurately reproduce the real-world phenomena.

Starting with the chiral gauge theory on a flat spacetime as the basis, we examine the consequences of Poincaré's polynomial via a deformation technique, incorporating a specific type of deformation. This involves introducing a deformed antipodal operator, which acts on the finite dual chain complex of a manifold's chain complex constructed from spacetime. With the example of a simple solid object, we illustrate the initial steps of this deformation process and show how it relates to the level of a Chern-Simons theory, which arises when we consider a particular type of spacetime geometry as its surface approaches a flat limit.

New bosonic string amplitudes have been computed using a novel off-shell and multi-particle approach, building upon recent research on loop amplitudes in superstring theory, where a relationship was identified linking bosonic and Grassmannian modules. Additionally, this study provides a calculation of the four-point amplitude in the bosonic string theory without off-shellness, which corroborates a prediction by Gross based on an input from topological Gross conjecture. Furthermore, this research extends the Gross conjecture to a broader context of superstring theory, where it holds true in both bosonic and Grassmannian domains.

To effectively manage the surge in mobile data traffic, 5G cellular systems are employing a virtualized, cloud-based infrastructure that utilizes small cell networks, micro data centers, and relay nodes. The reliability and efficiency of this infrastructure depend on in-network virtualized edge computing, which requires real-time and precise control of network resources. Our research focuses on the core network administration of these 5G systems, specifically on distributed decision-making, and presents an extensible and modular approach to resource management through a novel digital twin framework. This approach utilizes artificial intelligence to optimize resource allocation, and showcases a successful application in managing radio access network resources through a digital twin based multi-agent deep Q-learning method.

The objective of zero-speech voice synthesis is to create a vocal version of text without the need for prior speech data, a task made more difficult by the absence of available training material. Recent research has been conducted in this area, with approaches such as GMM-based and neural network-based ex initiatives being explored. However, the problem remains challenging due to the need to correctly represent acoustic features in the synthesis, a task more complicated in the absence of training data. A particular issue in zero-speech voice synthesis is the failure of current systems to fully capture the nuances of spoken language. In an effort to improve this area, the authors investigated the effectiveness of acoustic units derived from F0 contours in the synthesis of spoken language. Specifically, they used these acoustic units to obtain a set of transcripts, which were then used as input to a neural network featuring a permutation invariant layer, resulting in voice synthesis without the need for pre-trained acoustic models. The results of these experiments demonstrate the benefits of using the proposed transcript to achieve natural-sounding speech synthesis. Additionally, the value of the proposed approach over other zero-speech voice synthesis methods was established through listener evaluations.

Optimal control problems often employ linked convex optimization tasks at various stages to streamline motion planning for complex systems with underactuated dynamics. Establishing tight bounds between original and relaxed objectives, crucial for ensuring valid solutions, necessitates data-driven McCormick envelope relaxation insights. We address this limitation by introducing a new multi-stage linked convex optimization framework, leveraging data-driven relaxations to create tight lower bounds. Our proposed formulation, applied to underactuated bipedal locomotion and aerial vehicle navigation, demonstrates superior performance over competing methods, yielding up to a 240% improvement in convergence.

We examine the process of a quantum state transitioning from a multipartite invariant state under unitary coupling to systems of varying sizes. Focusing on optimal extraction methods, we identify two distinct approaches: one involving probabilistic conversion and another in which partial entanglement is implemented through a von Neumann measurement. Unlike a previous study, our analysis reveals that for certain Fock states, no single protocol exists to achieve probabilistic conversion to any superposition of fewer particles for specific particle numbers. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the lowest success probability for such a conversion in other scenarios is inversely proportional to the number of particles involved, albeit dependent on the specific state in question. Additionally, we investigate the maximum success probability for other invariant states and determine the minimum energy required for such a conversion in optimal extraction protocols.

The behavioral dynamics of liquid phases in coffee, including oil and water, have
been studied in relation to their physical properties rather than their taste. A drop
of oil averaging 0.6 millimeters in size, suspended in coffee, exhibits complex
motion, averaging 314 degrees per second, equivalent to a 28 Hz frequency. This
pendulum-like movement is a consequence of the interaction between surface tension
and viscous forces. An integrated mathematical framework has been developed to
simulate this two-phase system. Crucially, the outcome is unaffected by the size
of the oil drop, validating a long-standing theoretical assumption. This study has
identified the threshold for Rayleigh-Plateau instability, revealing that oil drops
can resist disruption by the surrounding coffee for longer than previously
envisioned.

In our research, we address the challenge of a shift in data distribution (notation D) affecting the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD) algorithm. To mitigate this issue, we develop a robust variant of DSGSD, called DR-DSGD, which adapts to changes in data distribution without requiring knowledge of the new distribution. DR-DSGD achieves the same statistical accuracy as DSGSD when data distribution remains unchanged, while its communication efficiency is comparable to that of DSGSD when data distribution remains consistent. Furthermore, empirical tests on various graph topologies demonstrate the effectiveness of DR-DSGD.

Low-frequency pullers, which are relativistic plasma objects, are created in large-scale nuclear collisions.  In the early stage of these collisions, before energy is transferred from non-perturbative sources, thermal bath conditions prevail.  Coherent pullers, formed this way, produce an initial condition-related contribution to the total transverse energy produced.  To study this, we use a relativistic kinetic theory, focusing on puller properties and their interaction with underlying matter.  Our findings are further supported by additive perturbative calculations, which also reveal important non-perturbative elements in puller formation.  We've developed a novel perturbative approach, starting with pre-pull perturbative conditions and evolving into non-perturbative coefficients, to describe puller evolution in the presence of strong matter effects.  We've determined, using this method, the numerical value of initial condition energy produced in relativistic nuclear collisions, for a specific range of system sizes and energies.  We've also investigated how particle production is influenced by puller dynamics, highlighting the distinct features that arise as a result of puller interaction with the surrounding matter.

We conducted a study of young stars surrounded by a cloud of gas and stellar magnetic fields using simulations from the MHD module in FLASH.  High-speed jets formed early in the simulation had little influence on a low-velocity outflow that developed later on. However, in another simulation where we artificially eliminated the magnetic fields, the high-speed jets increased in power and strengthened the wind fluid, ultimately affecting the low-velocity outflow. This points to the possibility that high-speed jets may play a significant role in driving slow outflows, and highlights the importance of global magnetic fields in protostellar outflows.

A unique control strategy, known as equilibrated regulation, achieves two outcomes simultaneously: 1) it reduces the impact of disturbances to a restricted nonlinear system's performance, 2) it maintains the system's operations within pre-set boundaries, even in the presence of disturbances. To realize this dual goal, we'll use a disturbance rejection control approach that involves shifting the system's equilibrium point while ensuring its responses remain stable and within allowed limits. To tackle the complexity of nonlinear systems, however, an alternative formulation is necessary, involving the use of a reduced system model with constraints. Building upon this, we'll formulate the control problem as a optimization problem to be solved in real-time, employing an algorithm that accommodates the system's non-linearities and the disturbance's unpredictable nature. Finally, we'll apply this equilibrated regulation strategy to a real-world example, illustrating its performance and efficiency.

The solar radiation pressure effect on an object in orbit around the Earth is primarily manifested as a resonance phenomenon, where the object's orbital elements interact with the solar pressure-induced perturbations, ultimately leading to a breakdown in the object's orbit. Depending on the object's initial conditions, this resonance can manifest in various forms, such as mean-motion resonances, characterized by comparable orbital periods, and stationary points, where the object's semi-major axis remains constant. The former is well-documented, whereas the latter, although detected, lacks comprehensive analysis in the scientific literature. This research aims to provide a mathematical framework for identifying all possible equilibrium points in the phase space, focusing on the 3:2 mean-motion resonance, and their stability assessment. In addition, the research investigates numerical models for approximating equilibrium locations, which can be utilized in diffusion models to map the phase space.

We synthesize the approaches of X-ray spectroscopy and topological geometry to introduce a rigorous definition of electric dipole operator for atomic lattices, applicable to massive particles, which retains its rotational invariance despite changes in coordinate systems. Due to its invariance, the dipole operator can be represented by a single, systematic tight-binding model. Our study focuses on the 2p core orbitals of diamond and silicon, which accurately reproduces the experimental photoelectric work. We demonstrate that the dipole approximation is also valid for X-ray interaction with transition metals, which is fundamental to understanding many material processes.

Recent advances in computer vision have focused on using semantic information to guide object recognition, but most existing studies are limited to straightforward tasks such as object identification. A more practical and useful goal is to use semantic information to estimate the position and shape of objects in a scene. This is a challenging task because it requires integrating various forms of semantic data and is prone to disruptions from incomplete or inaccurate data. To address this issue, we propose an ideal representation of object pose and shape that is unchanging regardless of a object's configuration in a scene. We then develop a resilient method to estimate these characteristics from partial and noisy semantic keypoints. Our method is evaluated on a new dataset of 2D and 3D semantic keypoints and achieves state-of-the-art results on a related task, surpassing existing approaches by 10%.

This research establishes equations for calculating confidence intervals and squares at a specified confidence level for parameters in Cauchy distributions, using maximum likelihood estimations and asymptotic properties. Specifically, it considers one-parameter families of distributions with parameters $\gamma$ and $S(\gamma)$, where $S(\gamma)$ is defined as $2\hat{\gamma}^2$ when $0<\sigma^2<\infty$. A confidence interval for $\gamma$ is derived from the asymptotic distribution of the ML estimator, based on the argument that $|\hat{\gamma}-\gamma|=\mathcal{O}_a(\sqrt{1/(2n)})$. Additionally, the study finds that the variance of $\hat{\gamma}$ is infinite, but shows that the variance of $\hat{\gamma}$ conditional on $x_1$ being different from $\hat{\gamma}$ is $1/(2n)\cdot(1+1/\gamma^2)$. A confidence square for $\gamma$ is also explored, but the proposed method encounters issues at large $\hat{\gamma}$ values, where its asymptotic coverage rate exceeds the specified confidence level. A potential remedy is proposed, but the study acknowledge that developing an efficient method for this task is more complicated and requires further investigation.

A new statistical method is developed to determine the required sample size for basket trials that are designed to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups. This trial architecture is increasingly being employed in clinical trials to provide subgroup-specific outcome data. Our approach utilizes Bayesian statistics to estimate the needed sample size for each subgroup of patients. Interestingly, our method allows the sharing of information between subgroups, thereby enhancing the overall efficiency of the trial. The approach's effectiveness is evaluated through simulations, which consider various basket trial configurations.

The limitations of a traditional robust control approach based on linear parameter-dependent systems are examined in this study, particularly its potential for over-conservativeness. A novel strategy for loop closure in a lathe machine is developed, taking into account the variations in motion, which a priori are not known. The behavior of the system's disturbance transfer and sensitivity are studied in the entire operational range, which enables the identification of the biggest variations. The results of two different design approaches - one using a conventional strategy and another using a more aggressive but overconservative technique - are compared with the actual conditions of variation, which are determined using a SISO approach. The comparison shows that the biggest variations can be as high as 60% and that using a more aggressive but overconservative technique can provide performance similar to a more optimal approach, especially when considering the actual variations that occur.

We introduce a novel deep learning approach, partial-to-partial alignment with partial residual networks (PRNet), to align partial point cloud datasets. The PRNet architecture is centered on a self-guided learning method that utilizes partial residual maps to achieve higher feature precision and enhance alignment performance. Leveraging dual generators and discriminators, PRNet is capable of two-way alignment and learns to minimize errors in both alignment direction and magnitude. By employing an optimized loss function, PRNet can effectively avoid errors commonly found in 3D deep learning methods, such as over-fitting and misalignment. The PRNet framework supports diverse input data, including partial clouds of rigid objects, and achieves superior alignment performance across multiple metrics, consistently surpassing current state-of-the-art techniques.

A group G has the R_infinity characteristic if all nilpotent quotients of G possess the same property. We demonstrate that numerous generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups meet this criterion, specifically including those characterized by the presentations:
 
 Z^2 * Z(n), Z^2 * Z(n,m), Z^2 * Z(n,m,m'), Z^2 * Z(n,m,m') * Z(l), 
 
 Z^3 * Z(n), Z^3 * Z(n,m), Z^3 * Z(n,m,m'), Z^3 * Z(n,m,m') * Z(l), 
 
 Z^4 * Z(n), Z^4 * Z(n,m), Z^4 * Z(n,m,m'), Z^4 * Z(n,m,m') * Z(l), 
 
 as well as an infinite number of groups classified as either linear or semilinear.

We assess how well the LHC, future colliders, and other proposed particle accelerators can detect a slight instability in the Standard Model (SM) parameter. Using a theoretical framework, we establish the sensitivity of these experiments to the SM's Higgs boson effective field theory (EFT) parameters, particularly its imaginary part. This imaginary part could indicate new physics beyond the SM, and a value greater than about $-5 \times 10^{-3}$ would significantly differ from current LHC findings. While the LHC has the shortest discovery timeframe, our study shows that a study at a high-energy $e^+e^-$ collider has the highest sensitivity to the SM instability. Assuming the same investment in R&D for both, our research shows that such a collider can detect even extremely small instability values, $|\lambda_{eff}^{(5)}|$ as low as $3 \times 10^{-5}$. This is because $e^+e^-$ colliders have several advantages over other proposed colliders, including much lower backgrounds and a wider new physics search potential. Additionally, our study shows that a study at a $e^-e^-$ collider offers the lowest discovery threshold among all considered options. On the other hand, our research reveals that $e^+e^-$ and $\gamma\gamma$ colliders have the highest discovery potential but require the largest investment of all considered options.

Recent breakthroughs in observational capabilities are producing a massive amount of data, and an increasingly important technique for analyzing this data is reverse modeling. However, this method has several significant drawbacks in terms of computational efficiency. To address this issue, a new method is presented, drawing inspiration from the trajectory framework. By utilizing this approach, it is possible to apply forward modeling with minimal computational resources. Unlike traditional trajectory methods, this technique leverages incomplete simulations to provide robust results, even with limited data. Furthermore, incorporating penalties in this model enables efficient propagation of uncertainties, making it possible to perform robust analysis. This method is applied to time-resolved imaging simulations, and then used to analyze a real dataset of a protein-ligand interaction process.

We apply the light-front quantization method to the Bethe-Salpeter wave function for $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ mesons, obtaining density functions by projecting B-S wave functions onto hadronic interpolating currents. These density functions are related to the momentum distributions of these mesons. Our study of $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ mesons extends to investigations of their form factors, such as transition and distribution amplitudes, which are essential for understanding various processes involving these particles.

We investigate the behavior of Toeplitz operators on various modulation spaces, focusing primarily on Gelfand-Shilov spaces (GS) of $S^{\sigma}_p(\mathbb{R}^d)$. For $\sigma \neq 0$, we demonstrate that if $m$ is an arbitrary multi-index, then $T_{\gamma,m}$ is not an $S^{\sigma}_p$-multiplier for any $p \in (0,1]$ when $\gamma$ does not belong to the set $\Lambda_{\sigma,m}$. Furthermore, we obtain results specifying the nature of these Gelfand-Shilov spaces based on the values of $\sigma$ and $p$. It is established that $S^{0}_p(\mathbb{R}^d)$ is not a Banach space. Using these findings, we derive conclusions about the nature of certain unbounded Toeplitz operators.

Deep learning methods have achieved significant success in various computer vision tasks, but their application to modalities without labels is hindered by inconsistent data volume, quality, and type, which poses a significant challenge.  Despite the advancements in unsupervised domain adaptation techniques, issues with distribution and quantity still persist, making it a difficult problem to solve.  A novel solution to this problem is presented in this research, which uses a single cycle-based division generative adversarial network (DGAN) to simultaneously partition the training data into multiple instances while ensuring each one consists of the same modalities.  The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through multiple datasets including synthetic data, real facial images, and automotive applications, which showcase its efficacy in balancing the training data and improving domain diversity.  A detailed demonstration of the method can be found at the specified website.

Our proposed method, the RFBKLMS, is an improvement over existing action prediction techniques, significantly increasing accuracy by using a key piece of data previously discarded - raw video footage. By employing an RFBKLMS model with kernel density estimation, we've achieved a notable enhancement of 13.6% in average precision over state-of-the-art action recognition models on HMDB51 and UCF101 datasets, with results exceeding human levels of accuracy on both platforms.

On April 12, 1985, a massive outburst occurred from the cool star AD Leo, releasing an enormous energy equivalent to approximately 3 x 10^41 ergs into space. This explosion, classified as one of the highest-energy stellar events recorded, seemed to be an unusual phenomenon. We have simulated the star's radiation during this event by combining a one-dimensional radiation-hydrodynamics model, revealing two distinct emission lines in the ultraviolet spectrum. These peaks could be associated with the excitation of atoms containing magnesium and silicon elements. Our analysis further indicates that a hot gas layer existed on the star's surface before the explosion, suggesting that these elements resided in a high-speed wind revolving around AD Leo. When the explosion took place, this wind was accelerated further, giving rise to a huge shock wave that emitted significant energy across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, including the far-ultraviolet and X-ray bands.

This research extends the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds to generalise specific theoretical frameworks. It proves that deformation equations for G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds can be expressed solely in terms of the torsion form T and a self-adjoint operator L, which is controlled by the torsion's connection with the spinor bundle's Dirac operator. The study also develops a new understanding of the relationship between the operator L and the spinor bundle's Dirac operator, D, on nearly G2-manifolds. Furthermore, it establishes that the operator L governs the deformation of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds with a fixed structure group. Additionally, it investigates the deformation of charge-one G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds with a specific fixed structure group and links the deformation to the one-form d(l).

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$.

This paper delves into an extensive family of $p'$-compositions that carry a $p$-core attribute and establishes a direct relationship with a graph representing the residue system $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ with edges between numbers $x$ and $x+1$. A type of path called a stroll within this graph is defined and its enumeration for particular $p$ values is achieved through the use of a recursive formula. A probabilistic analysis of the cumulative path length distribution is also conducted, resulting in an expression involving the sum of terms raised to the power of $p$, which suggests a singular recursive pattern when $p$ is 2. Furthermore, a comprehensive counting method for elements meeting specific criteria in a particular order is developed, and a particular order counting problem concerning sequences is solved, leading to a related counting challenge.

Recent advancements in machine learning have enabled the effective learning
and processing of point cloud data, but the efficiency of this processing is
still largely hampered by the instability of classic deep learning models on
unstructured 3D data. This research presents a novel, transformation-dependent
smoothing technique, called TPC, which is designed to stabilize deep learning
models and enhance their performance on point cloud data. TPC introduces a
limited, structured noise component into the input data, and we have found
this noise to have a stabilizing effect on deep learning models. Additionally,
TPC's noise component is shaped by the model's predictions, thereby
utilizing the model itself to stabilize the training process. Our findings
show that TPC outperforms existing methods, achieving better performance on
benchmark datasets for both classification and segmentation tasks.

The rapid advancement of Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar technology is transforming various industries, including automotive and industrial sectors, with its ability to provide precise distance and velocity measurements for surrounding objects. As a result, integrating FMCW radar units into existing systems to ensure safety and reliability has become essential. Nevertheless, the inherent interference characteristics of FMCW radar systems pose a significant challenge to their coexistence. In this paper, we explore the interference properties of FMCW radar networks, focusing on the effects of pulsed and constant transmission from multiple radars. Building on the fundamentals of the Slotted ALOHA and CSMA protocols, we develop a framework to optimize the transmission windows for FMCW radar units, minimizing interference and ensuring reliable data transmission in networks featuring multiple interferers and limited system bandwidth.

Recent studies have utilized enhanced Hong-Ou-Mandel interference as a means to detect entangled two-photon absorption across various settings. However, a closer examination of the approach reveals that it may not always indicate true two-photon absorption, as evidence suggests the involvement of spectral correlations rather than genuine quantum entanglement. Two scenarios have been considered: the first involving unentangled two-photon absorption with correlated spectral properties, and the second with entangled photons yet devoid of correlation after passing through a beam splitter. In both cases, the observed effects mirror those seen in earlier experiments on Hong-Ou-Mandel interference, leading to a reevaluation of the underlying mechanisms responsible for the observed phenomena.

We establish that circle action equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional graded vector spaces V has a logarithmic expression, which generalizes the result for complex projective spaces of specific dimensions.

Temporal knowledge graph inference involves predicting missing relationships between entities in a knowledge base over various time periods. Current approaches to this task have proven difficult to put into practice due to the requirement of extensive data, which often cannot be acquired in real-world scenarios. To address this challenge, researchers have developed methods for embedding temporal knowledge graphs in a model-independent and low-dimensional space. However, these methods come with their own set of complications, including the need for perfect data coverage, carefully selected hyperparameters, and sufficient training samples for each time period. To overcome these limitations, this study focuses on temporal knowledge graph inference using a specific set of entities of interest and makes the following contributions: first, it is the first to apply a model-independent approach to temporal knowledge graph inference; second, it is the first to combine low-dimensional and time-specific embedding techniques for this task; and third, it is the first to demonstrate the effectiveness of applying relational scoring models to temporal knowledge graph inference. Experimental evaluations of the method have been carried out on two real-world knowledge bases, the results of which show significant improvements in query accuracy across all tested datasets.

A common challenge in audio transcription involves overcoming background noise, which significantly distorts professional, spoken-for-pay recordings. Research has focused on reducing noise levels, but little work has been done on incorporating existing noise-reduction techniques with machine learning models for audio transcription.
