Nonetheless, the current batch-based implementation is hindered by the lack of complete data access, poor handling of non-local data, and an unsuitable scoring function. To overcome these problems, this research presents User-Centric Bicluster-based CF (UCBCF), a real-time, adaptive framework that maintains complete data access, accurately identifies both user and item preferences, and incorporates rating significance. The system's performance in addressing these challenges will be evaluated using real-world datasets, including movies and documents.

Recent high-precision sunspotless observations from HARPS-N discovered previously unknown spectral features in the sun's spectrum, shifting our understanding of the sun's surface activity. High-resolution solar spectra in the near-infrared and visible ranges were affected in areas with sunspots and faculae, as detected by SDO and HMI imagery. Faculae, thought to display magnetic behavior distinct from sunspots, influenced the sun's spectrum in a unique way. In order to better understand this, researchers used the sun as a target to investigate how magnetic features such as the strength of magnetic field, convective area, and temperature influence variations in solar spectra. A comprehensive analysis of sunless spectra, along with spotless faculae, enabled researchers to develop new indicators of the sun's magnetic activity. These indicators can also be applied to other stars, and are expected to provide significant insight into the connection between solar surface features and stellar activity.

In probing Majorana modes, identifying a peak in tunneling conductance is crucial, yet distinguishing it from other peaks is a significant challenge. Our proposed technique aims to resolve this issue and provides a systematic method to eliminate three major sources of contamination peaks through analytical and numerical methods. By utilizing a simple setup with a resistive electrode and ohmic dissipation, we have developed a tunneling characterization method that leverages the unique properties of Majorana modes to define a "Majorana region" on a conductance map. Our analysis, backed by numerical simulations, demonstrates that common experimental setups can effectively eliminate common contaminants to pinpoint the Majorana peak accurately.

Mark Kisin initially proposed the concept of B-categorical marks as a localized version of the Mark Kisin's B-marks introduced in his 2007 paper 'Twisted self-products and endomorphisms'. In 2021, Matthew Ghoul and Michael Schein further developed this concept, exploring B-categorical marks in relation to twisted self products. Building upon these prior works, we present an alternative approach to B-categorical marks, specifically for the case of Shimura varieties of finite type. Within this context, we demonstrate that B-categorical marks can be expressed as the B-marks multiplied by the zeroth Galois cohomology class of an appropriate sheaf, depending on the case at hand. In addition, we establish several key findings. Firstly, B-categorical marks are 1-marks. Secondly, B-categorical marks are B-marks if and only if they are B-marks of twisted self products. Thirdly, B-categorical marks do not necessarily correspond to B-marks of the twisted varieties themselves. Lastly, we illustrate our findings through examples.

Our objective is to remove excessive contrast from high dynamic range images, a process known as tone mapping. We've developed two approaches, one forwarding and one reversing, to achieve this. Forward tone mapping converts HDR images to more human-friendly LDR images using a style transfer of local features from a training database of HDR images. This style transfer involves two processes - mapping pixels to nearest neighbors and applying non-linear encoding to achieve desired LDR images. In contrast, reverse tone mapping uses a neural network to extract a global style from LDR images, which is then used to generate HDR images. We've tested these methods on various scenes and real-world images, producing favorable results.

This technical report outlines the rules and evaluation protocol for the AQTC task in the LOVEU contest held at CVPR 2022. It details the objectives, constraints, and assessment criteria of the competition.

Our research focuses on the formation of cloud layers through the fall of snowflakes, 
which is a key process in developing clouds that ultimately affect the Earth's 
energy balance. Using advanced imaging technologies to monitor snowflake motion, 
we uncover a two-stage process: a initial swift movement towards the layer's 
midpoint followed by a slower, more intricate dancing-like behavior in the core 
region. This pattern arises due to the interaction of snowflakes utilizing various 
shapes to navigate through the atmosphere's irregular temperature patterns. 
Typically, the swift movement is a result of snowflakes using their projections as 
aerial brakes, slowing their descent with an abrupt shift in flight, an action 
that temporarily positions them at the core. Subsequently, they participate in 
a complex dance, shifting in response to their size, shape, and bracing patterns, 
where the differentiation into the upper and lower core regions develops over time, 
ultimately leading to their classification into distinct groups based on their motion. 
This two-stage process represents a breakthrough in the understanding of selective 
sweeping and is expected to significantly contribute to the field of atmospheric 
turbulence.

This research introduces a novel approach to robot navigation, focusing on an environment where no prior map is available. The agent's goal is to explore the space using an built-in purpose, such as finding a specific object, and making its own decisions without external guidance. A unified framework called Profound Active Deduction (PAD) is proposed to achieve this objective. PAD leverages Deduction Graphs to generate both action and Policy options, based on the latest knowledge update. By incorporating self-monitoring, PAD can assess the quality of its own decisions, using the expected outcome in relation to the current situation. A simulation test has been conducted to verify the efficiency of PAD in comparison to other widely-used methods.

In recent years, the development of Tape-Drive-Particle-Counters has accelerated research in multiple fields, including atmospheric science and space exploration. Traditional particle counters using circular grids have limitations in detecting large particles and are prone to occlusion effects. The three-dimensional tape design provides a higher detection capacity and resolves the occlusion issue, but it also presents a complex data problem. Specifically, the 3D tape structure generates sparse, high-dimensional data with significant inter-channel correlations. Given these challenges, data reduction techniques are in high demand to streamline analysis and boost processing efficiency while maintaining data quality. In response to these needs, this research introduces a Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE) model that directly addresses the complexities of 3D TPC data through an autoencoding approach. The BCAE model comprises two autoencoders working in tandem to learn the spatial patterns in TPC data, resulting in a reduced-dimensional representation that preserves important data features. Experimental results on actual spacecraft data validate the BCAE model's capability to compress data while maintaining relevant information, outperforming conventional methods.

In the Finzi gravitation model, where gravity resembles electromagnetic forces, we have studied galaxy clusters developing within a homogenous, expansive universe. Our research finds that, unlike in General Relativity, the shapes of galaxy clusters in the Finzi model follow Roche types, with their profiles mirroring those of isolated stars. Notably, we have demonstrated that the distribution of the radial distances of galaxies within clusters follows a Boltzmann distribution, analogous to the Hubble volume scenario. Additionally, we have shown that the masses of galaxy clusters within the Finzi model follow a power-law distribution, which contrasts with the log-normal distribution observed in General Relativity. Our findings have significance as they offer insights into the unique characteristics of galaxy clusters forming within a universe governed by the Finzi gravitation model.

A type of geometric hypergraph called cGH(n,d) consists of a collection of subsets containing at most d points each, characterized by being convex in a d-dimensional space. Research has demonstrated that for a geometric hypergraph meeting these criteria, its H-rebarr(d) value will be roughly n^(1/(2+ε)) if d is three or greater. Here, H-rebarr(d) represents the maximum number for a geometric hypergraph under such constraints that can be formed using a value 'r' for a specific k, resulting in points arranged in a geometric fashion. Investigating this area of study, we identify cGH(n,4) instances where the H-rebarr(4) value reaches n^(1/3). This research also explores the challenges associated with proving a theoretical upper limit for geometric hypergraphs, even with simplified convex geometries.

To study direct neutron resonance capture and other alternative proton capture processes, the $^6$Li+$^51$V system was investigated. Using a merged-beams technique, experimental cross-sections for $^6$Li + $^51$V elastic scattering and breakup were obtained. These data, combined with theoretical calculations based on the finite range distorted wave Born approximation, led to the derivation of inclusive $\alpha$ cross-sections. The calculated inclusive $\alpha$ cross-sections matched the experimental results, and the obtained angular distributions and energy spectra showed characteristics typical of compound nuclear effects, indicating that high-lying states of the compound nucleus $^57$Ta were involved. Additionally, the analysis of the angular distributions and energy spectra of the fragments suggested the existence of two distinct nuclear states at excitation energies above the $^{57}$Ta ground state.

A study investigated the neural mechanisms behind an ascending motor reflex in Pacific lampreys, which involves a complex process where sensory input from touch stimulates a specific part of the brain, leading to increased brain areas being active in succession and ultimately results in the contraction of specific muscles in the lamprey's trunk. This reflex relies on a specific part of the brain, called the dorsal root vesicle, which receives sensory input from the central nervous system and sends signals to another part, the mesencephalic nucleus of the vagus, to initiate muscle contraction. To understand this process further, researchers used electrophysiology to record the responses of individual neurons within specific groups, such as the vesicle's interneurons, which receive input from the central nervous system, and primary sensory neurons, which transmit touch information to the vesicle, as well as excitatory neurons that send signals to the vagus nucleus. This study's findings provide new insights into the underlying neural processes behind this reflex and the structure of the Pacific lamprey's central nervous system, which is notable for its relatively simple layout, making it a useful model for understanding vertebrate neural motivations and reflexes.

We develop a novel framework to create an effective immune response against colon cancer by customizing immunotherapy treatment. To start, we model the dynamics of the tumor's interaction with the immune system using the Fokker-Planck equation, which governs the distribution of T cells over time and space. This interaction is influenced by various factors, such as the levels of cytokines and antigens present. Building upon this, we formulate a control problem to maximize the probability of the tumor's destruction by optimizing the release of cytokines from cytokine-augmentation locations. This control problem adheres to certain feasibility constraints to ensure realistic immune response dynamics. To address the non-trivial nature of solving the Fokker-Planck equation and the associated optimal control problem, we develop a sequence of successive approximations to obtain custom-made treatment strategies, which can be rapidly calculated. These customized treatments are individualized, data-driven methods that rely on real-time patient data to optimize the immune response.

The Wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication method holds great promise for efficient use of cellular spectrum. However, implementing an optimal scheduling system that considers interference and data transfer rates in large D2D networks is a major challenge. Traditional methods using mathematical optimization and game theory have limitations in scalability and complexity. To address this issue, a new method is proposed that uses deep learning to develop a self-optimizing wireless scheduling scheme for large D2D networks. This approach exploits patterns in the problem through deep neural networks, enabling efficient design and scalability for complex problems. A wide range of D2D network configurations can be efficiently handled using this method, which outperforms traditional scheduling techniques by maximizing overall network capacity under specific performance metrics.

We begin by establishing a definition of helicity for a compressible fluid, then prove that it remains constant over time for a barotropic fluid with smooth, non-flat interface within a fixed domain, excluding the boundary, using a variational derivative approach. This result can be extended to conserve mass and energy for a barotropic fluid with a smooth, bounded interface and to conserve helicity for a non-barotropic fluid with a smooth interface. Additionally, we demonstrate that the helicity is preserved in the presence of a potential force in both barotropic and non-barotropic fluids. These findings apply to both two-dimensional and three-dimensional flows.

For the Davey-Stewartson II equations, the reflection coefficient of a specific nonlinear Schrödinger equation derived from multiconfocal nonlinear Schrödinger equations has been calculated, and its behavior, particularly at large values of $k$, has been examined. This investigation draws on the newly developed large-$|k|$ approach and reveals an unexpected feature: the presence of a singular point within the reflection coefficient's logarithmic derivative. As a result, the reflection coefficient does not follow the expected large-$|k|$ behavior. Instead, its real and imaginary parts exhibit distinct large-$|k|$ limits, which cannot be directly combined to yield a singular answer. Consequently, the large-$|k|$ approximation fails to yield a singular answer.

Merger events of compact objects such as neutron stars and black holes produce gravitational waves with amplitudes in the range of strains measured by ground-based detectors. The LIGO and Virgo Observatories have a sensitivity limit known as the residual eccentricity threshold (RET), which measures strain deviations from circular orbits. Our research aimed to estimate the ret for equal-mass binary black hole systems, starting with initial conditions including radial and highly eccentric orbits. We utilized accurate equations from post-Newtonian theory to model binary evolution. Our results indicate that roughly half of all detections come close to reaching the ret, leading to potential effects in data analysis. Conversely, binary black hole coalescence rates remain largely unaffected by eccentricity, accounting for less than 5 percent of variations. If the ret is lowered through upgraded equipment, the proportion of highly eccentric binary black hole coalescences could increase dramatically, reaching 30 percent in a potential future design. Our estimated binary black hole coalescence rates also suggest that neutron star-black hole mergers may be less common, occurring approximately 3 times less often than binary black hole coalescences in the ligo-virgo parameter space.

Achieving high luminosity and coherent X-ray levels is crucial for applications such as advanced imaging, high-pressure studies, and coherent imaging of biological samples.  A novel solution to produce high luminosity and coherent X-rays is proposed through combining a free-electron laser oscillator with a high-powered seed laser. The theoretical framework, supported by detailed simulations, demonstrates that by utilizing this approach it is possible to generate over 10^22 photons per second at a wavelength of 2 nm, with a high luminosity of 10^6 W cm^-2 and a low divergence of 10^-3 mrad. The proposed scheme has the potential to greatly enhance scientific research outcomes and could soon be realized with the advancement of next-generation soft X-ray enhancers.

In the rapidly changing world we live in, our connections with others evolve constantly, 
just like a career or a relationship. From the spread of viruses to political movements and 
 technological innovations, numerous processes are shaping our lives and our network. 
For instance, the virus that caused the Syrian uprising was the initial spark, 
while the U.S. Facebook revolution began with a single student's innovative idea. 
Understanding the origins and patterns of incidents like these, which are constantly unfolding, 
is vital for making informed decisions and predicting future developments. 
We're extracting insights from the intricate networks and making predictions 
using advanced techniques, all backed by solid mathematical foundations. 
Our focus is exploring how incidents spread and how we can identify their beginnings.

The shock wave collapses due to instability when it encounters a gradual density increase and flat pressure conditions. This phenomenon has significant implications in various astrophysical events, including massive star expansions into planetary nebulae and nuclear blast formations. This study employs a mathematical model, based on the Navier-Stokes equations, to investigate the dynamics of shock wave collapse in a medium with constantly changing density in two-dimensional space. To facilitate numerical computations, the researchers used a specialized algorithm to approximate the Navier-Stokes equations and evaluated the behavior of the shock wave, including its shape, position, and internal structures, in different scenarios. They also analyzed how these variables affect the final outcome of the shock wave collapse and conducted numerical experiments to validate their results.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted and solutions proposed, with a framework and future research directions on how requirements engineering can aid in the development of explainability specifications.

This study presents UniToPatho, a comprehensive dataset of colorectal polyp specimens derived from histological samples. The dataset comprises high-resolution digital images along with manually annotated regions of interest (ROIs) and expert pathology reports, making it suitable for deep learning-based approaches to identify and diagnose abnormal cell patterns. The training section of the dataset contains 13,226 images of annotated ROIs and 3,547 full-slide images, while the test section contains 1,106 images of annotated ROIs and 228 full-slide images. Notably, the dataset differs from other biomedical collections by incorporating images of the same patient from varying stages of the disease, as well as expert ratings on lesion borders to guide the training of segmentation models. The dataset demonstrates an optimal outcome for adenoma grading through a multi-task learning approach that simultaneously tackles classification and lesion grading during model training.

In the context of information theory, a unique data leakage model is explored, where a data sender attempts to encode information from a source without a pre-established code in place. Utilizing graph theory, the problem of efficient data encoding under these conditions is approached. Key findings reveal that data leakage can occur in any situation where the data sender's matrix does not have full column rank. Additionally, a general theory outlining the limits of leakage for arbitrary senders is developed. These theories are substantiated through several practical examples.

Deep learning techniques are widely adopted in synthetic aperture radar (SAR) image processing but often demand a large number of training examples, which can be costly to obtain. Moreover, the available data in remote sensing field typically suffers from data scarcity due to operational restrictions of the platforms. In this research, a novel hierarchical generative model named MrSARP is introduced to address the challenge of limited training data for super-resolution (SR) tasks using SAR images. The model is specifically designed with series Finch-Beta encoder to capture context-dependent correlations of low-resolution (LR) SAR images and generate high-resolution (HR) images through decoding process. The model's efficiency is evaluated using real-world data on SAR modules and the results show significant improvements over existing methods. Specifically, the model outperforms others by 8.1dB, 5.1dB and 3.6dB for various scales of LR images with 50%, 25%, and 12.5 reduction in resolution respectively.

A quantum approximate optimization algorithm variant incorporates variational principles from quantum chemistry into a classical optimization framework. We've developed a Bayesian extension to improve its performance, using probabilistic distributions to compensate for estimation errors in quantum circuit outcomes. The Bayesian method employs stochastic gradient ascent to optimize parameters and emerges as a special case of stochastic gradient variational Bayes learning. Experimental results on the QAOA variant demonstrate its superiority to the original approach, yielding significant time savings without compromising solution quality. The Bayesian method also produces more accurate approximate solutions than the classical and quantum annealing counterparts.

This research develops a method to identify areas where two or more ellipses intersect, which is crucial in various applications such as detecting biases in data and analyzing the movement of rigid bodies. The algorithm determines the types of intersection regions, whether it's area of overlap, a single point, or no intersection at all, using the characteristics of the intersecting areas. The method is also efficient as it operates on each pair of ellipses once, with a time complexity of O(k)s, where k represents the number of intersecting regions. To prove the algorithm's correctness, we utilize a hypothetical scenario where the combined area of the intersecting regions has a specific shape. This theoretical foundation allows us to verify that the algorithm accurately determines the types of intersection regions. The research further includes a set of test cases to demonstrate that the algorithm can handle a variety of real-world scenarios, as well as a performance analysis that highlights the method's efficiency.

The concept of q-training is particularly useful in an ongoing learning setting, allowing for the update of a model's parameters at any point in time without requiring a complete data batch. Our theoretical analysis provides a framework for understanding when a model can be efficiently updated using this approach, especially when dealing with non-stationary data. We also examine the practical implications of q-training, highlighting its ability to mitigate the effects of data imbalance and enhance feature representation. Our experimental results, which focus on background subtraction using Background-Inherent Gaussian Mixture Models, demonstrate the effectiveness of this method and showcase its utility as a background pre-processing tool.

Our analysis, based on a self-consistent functional renormalization group approach, reveals the interplay of multiple magnetic phases in a triangular-lattice Hubbard model with next-nearest-neighbor interactions.  The phase diagram exhibits not only a quantum magnetic transition from an anti-ferromagnetic to a spin-density wave phase, but also a transition to a completely resonating multi-spin singlet ground state through an intermediate phase of chaotic magnetic correlations.  The onset of magnetic disorder is observed to be induced by the competition between nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor interactions, which interacts synergistically with the properties of the electronic Green's function.  Notably, our findings for the entanglement entropy as a function of system size and interaction strength aligns with the theoretical predictions of quantum magnetic transitions based on entanglement entropy scaling laws.

In this research, a combination of vertebral spinelining and anatomically-restricted optimization was applied to identify and position the vertebrae on computed tomography (CT) scans with low resolution and low contrast. By initially rotating the CT image to align with the spinal axis, the center of the first lumbar vertebra was located using a circular mask, followed by a segmentation method that encloses all vertebrae using a Riemannian camera movement. A combination of vertebral shape and position constraints was applied to a global optimization algorithm to precisely position each vertebra. A distance metric based on center-to-center distance and vertebral width was used to evaluate solutions. A global optimization algorithm was applied to identify the best fit for the vertebrae. In our experiments, 95% of the time, the algorithm accurately located all L4 vertebrae within 0.4mm and 0.6mm in axial and lateral directions respectively, with an average localization time of 21.2 milliseconds, 94% of the time, the algorithm accurately located all L5 vertebrae within 0.4mm and 0.6mm in axial and lateral directions respectively, with an average localization time of 21.4 milliseconds, and the method automatically detected and positioned all vertebrae without the need for manual adjustment in 30 CT scans.

We've developed a random thermodynamic framework that allows us to derive probability distributions for various physical parameters, such as electric and magnetic field spectral densities. Notably, our method respects gauge invariance, as demonstrated through the consideration of two specific cases: (1) fluctuating magnetic field in a two-dimensional superconductor and (2) electric field in a charged Dirac fermion system near a topological boundary. The derived distributions can be measured experimentally and provide unique insights into critical properties of these systems. We've also formulated a universal gauge-invariant relationship, applicable to all gyromagnetic systems, that's relevant to the analysis of NMR, muon spin resonance, and other types of magnetic measurements. This relationship incorporates key system parameters, such as the system's susceptibility and electron spin properties.

This research examines how rational transformations impact relative quantum homology in the context of a specific class of symplectic mappings. Building on earlier work by de Sarlo, we expand upon his findings, considering more comprehensive scenarios. Our key contribution lies in the development of a novel quantum product for the relative homology group of a symplectic right-coset space, mapped via a rational transformation $\phi$. Furthermore, we identify the $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra structure of the relative quantum cohomology ring, and demonstrate that $\phi$ generates an auto-equivalence of the derived category of $\mathbb{Q}$-valued chains on the symplectic right-coset space, with the latter being equipped with its natural $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra structure.

The interaction between acoustic waves across the interface of two closely coupled piezoelectric materials is examined, and the conditions under which total transmission occurs are identified. When the coupled materials are monocrystalline and have the same polar orientation, acoustic waves transmit from one to the other without obstruction, and this transmission is attributed to the resonance facilitated by the formation of a hypothetically ideal junction. The crystalline structure allows for the transformation of an incident wave into a hyperbolic wave that can traverse the interface and be received by the second material as a transmitted wave. This transmission phenomenon offers a basis for the development of sensitive sensors capable of detecting even minute surface changes on piezoelectric materials.

We explore a novel method to create a photonic system utilizing an assembly of exciton-polariton emitters. A cavity contains two types of single photon sources: spin-dependent emitters and isotropic emitters. The emitters have a natural decay rate much faster than the cavity's, forming a non-equilibrium system that produces superradiance and photon correlations. Our research reveals that both emitters contribute to a steady-state photon flux and thermalization processes. Furthermore, we examine the auto-correlation function of photons escaping the cavity and find that it decays at an slower rate when both emitter types are present, indicating a longer-lived photonic interaction time. Our study provides insight into the optical properties of polariton assemblies and their potential application in photonic processing and information transfer at fast timescales.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b exhibits behaviors characteristic of both planetary bodies and debris disks, revealing the planet's composition and formation processes. Analyzing data from multiple observatories, researchers have detected changes in the planet's transmission spectra since its discovery in 2016. Combining observations from various facilities including SPitzer, Hubble, and LBT, they identify notable differences in the planet's spectrum, suggesting a higher rate of mass loss than previously predicted. Using models to compare observed and predicted data, researchers have found that the implied mass loss in favour of the higher rate exceeds 2 orders of magnitude. Additionally, researchers have found dust grains larger than expected, with upper bond ranging from 1-10 micrometers in size. Reducing the velocity of ejecta from 10km/s to as low as 1km/s has also been favoured. The new findings contradict prior flat or declining mass loss predictions and instead align with theory suggesting rapid changes in orbital position where the planet crosses through the warm inner region of its debris disk.

Garcia Prado and Searles previously established the Milnor fibration for complex singularities in certain situations, building on work by Namba and Ruediger, among others. A key component in their proof is the flatness of a specific singularity locus, and this paper explores the implications of this result, extending the principles of coherence and compatibility to the entire fibration.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analysis and numerical computations. Designed for.NET users, it offers data manipulation and visualization tools, as well as algorithm implementations for common mathematical and statistical applications. Developed atop the NetFramework 4.5, Daany is compatible with various.NET platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS.

The narrative that Galileo opposed philosophy has become entrenched in academic literature. This paper reexamines Galileo's views on the relationship between mathematics and philosophy, revealing them to be harmonious rather than contentious. Far from denigrating philosophy, Galileo saw mathematics as an integral component of the broader philosophical endeavor, particularly in the study of physics and theology. This is exemplified by his integration of mathematical methods in "The Assayer" and the concurrent development of his scientific and philosophical endeavors. This work argues that the myth of Galileo's antagonism towards philosophy stems from a misinterpretation of his criticism targeted at Scholasticism's failure to utilize mathematical methods, as well as a failure to distinguish between mathematics and philosophy in the Scholastic tradition.

The primary objective of this research is to examine the impact of Saha's ionization during the early stages of the universe, a process not yet thoroughly analyzed from a thermodynamic invariance standpoint. Building upon Nash's embedding theory, we've found that the Hubble parameter and neutrino temperature are unaffected by local Thomson scattering. However, contrary to expectations, we discovered that the Hubble parameter and neutrino temperature can be influenced by cosmic photons as a result of two-phase equilibrium. This finding may be attributed to the UV radiation's rapid displacement, a phenomenon that can be mitigated by utilizing Planck's black-body radiation instead of cosmic photons.

The theory of magnetic reconnection is receiving significant attention due to its widespread occurrence in various plasma environments, including astronomical bodies and man-made devices. Reconnection's pivotal role in many significant events, such as driving geomagnetic storms and powering solar flares, has furthered research in the field. Investigations of magnetic reconnection are often conducted using ultra-low frequency waves and their consequences, which can be effectively studied through simulations that employ magnetohydrodynamics. However, traditional MHD simulations may fail to capture critical aspects of reconnection that involve energetic particles interacting with the magnetic field. We address this limitation by integrating a PIC model dynamically into an MHD simulation, allowing for a more comprehensive examination of magnetic island formation and merging.

This research introduces Amanuensis, an innovative collaboration tool that supports human-in-the-loop as a machine learning model's instructor, drawing on ideas from human-computer interaction and educational theories. By embracing "trial and error" learning, Amanuensis empowers users to teach a Deep Neural Network (DNN) by providing input-output examples, even if the desired output is unclear or unspecified. Amanuensis was developed in response to the limitations of traditional learning methods, which often require precise output specifications. A case study demonstrating its effectiveness in text encoding was included in the paper.
